history: Hugo Ensslin printed it in 1916. When crème de violette left the US market, decades of bartenders served it without—and the drink lost its name-sake sky color.
whyItWorks: Maraschino brings funk and sweetness, violette brings perfume; the lemon keeps both from turning candied.
steps: Shake all liquid ingredients hard with ice.
techniqueNotes: Violette is a seasoning, not a base—past a quarter ounce it turns to soap.
Measure the maraschino carefully; Luxardo is far sweeter than it tastes.

recommendedBottles.rationale: Floral gin that meets the violette head-on.
Citrus-forward and cleaner if you want the lemon louder.

substitutions.notes: No true substitute. Omitting it gives you a Fancy Free-adjacent drink—honest, but not an Aviation.

name: Aviation
description: Gin, maraschino and a violet whisper—the pale-blue sour that vanished with its own liqueur.
